nameStory: This tiny grasshopper earned its "crested" name from the prominent ridge that runs along its back, like a miniature mountain crest. The "pygmy" part is obvious once you see one - these are among the smallest grasshoppers you'll encounter, living up to their diminutive name. Some folks also call them "grouse locusts," though they're neither grouse nor true locusts!
description: The Crested Pygmy Grasshopper is one of New England's tiniest hoppers, measuring less than half an inch long. These small, brown or grayish insects have a distinctive raised ridge or "crest" running down their back, giving them an almost armored appearance. Unlike their larger grasshopper cousins, pygmy grasshoppers have very short wings and do more walking and short hopping than dramatic leaping. They're often overlooked because of their small size and earth-toned coloring that blends perfectly with soil and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Prominent back crest
idTips.description: Look for the sharp, raised ridge running lengthwise down the center of the back - it feels firm to the touch and creates a distinctive triangular profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Barely reaches half an inch long, about the size of a small fingernail - you might mistake it for a beetle at first glance

idTips.label: Earth-tone coloring
idTips.description: Mottled brown, gray, or tan coloration that feels rough and textured, perfectly matching dried leaves and soil

idTips.label: Short, stubby antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are notably shorter than the head, unlike many other grasshoppers - they feel thin and thread-like when gently touched

idTips.label: Compact body shape
idTips.description: Stocky, compressed body that's wider than it is tall, with a solid, chunky feel when handled gently

habitat: Look for Crested Pygmy Grasshoppers in moist areas with bare soil or sparse vegetation, especially along stream banks, pond edges, and muddy trails. They favor spots where the ground stays damp but not waterlogged, often hiding among fallen leaves or in the spaces between rocks and roots. You'll also find them in marshy areas and wet meadows throughout New England's lowlands.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active on warm days, often seen basking on sun-warmed soil or rocks near water sources.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible and easiest to spot. They're actively feeding and mating, making them less skittish than in other seasons.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with new generation emerging. Look for them during warm afternoon hours before they seek winter shelter.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under logs, leaf litter, or in soil crevices. Occasionally spotted on unusually warm winter days emerging briefly to bask in sunlight.

funFact: Despite being called grasshoppers, these tiny creatures are actually better swimmers than jumpers - they can survive being completely submerged in water for several minutes and will dive underwater to escape predators, using their legs like tiny oars to swim to safety!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for small beetles or even aphids due to their tiny size and dark coloring. The key difference is their powerful hind legs (bent and ready to hop) and that distinctive back crest - beetles have hard wing covers instead of the grasshopper's triangular profile.
contextualKnowledge: The name "grouse locust" is confusing since these aren't locusts at all - true locusts are just grasshoppers that can swarm, and the "grouse" part simply refers to their ground-dwelling, earth-colored appearance similar to game birds. Pygmy grasshoppers belong to their own special family (Tetrigidae) and are quite different from the large, green grasshoppers most people picture.
compareHints: As the only Nomotettix species in New England, compare it to other pygmy grasshopper species in the region by looking for its particularly prominent, sharp-edged back crest. Other pygmy grasshoppers may have ridges or bumps, but none have quite the same knife-like crest that extends well beyond the abdomen. The Crested Pygmy Grasshopper's crest is also more triangular and pointed when viewed from behind compared to the more rounded profiles of its relatives.
